  <h1>Week 3: Markov Random Fields and Exact Inference</h1>

**Overview.** Week 2 built directed graphical models: pick an ordering of the variables, draw an arrow from each parent to each child, and read conditional independencies off the arrows. That works well when there is a natural causal or generative ordering, but many domains (a social network, a protein interaction network, the pixels of an image) have no natural direction to assign to an edge. This lecture introduces **Markov random fields (MRFs)**, undirected graphical models where an edge means "these two variables interact" rather than "one causes the other." We show what MRFs can express that DAGs cannot, and vice versa, then specialize to two concrete families: the Ising model (for discrete/binary variables) and Gaussian graphical models (for continuous ones), the latter directly useful for this course's first assignment. The second half turns to **exact inference**: given a graphical model, how do we actually compute a marginal or conditional probability without enumerating every possible assignment? **Variable elimination** answers this for both DAGs and MRFs at once, and we finish with a worked example and a modern application, the restricted Boltzmann machine.

## From DAGs to undirected graphs {#sec-motivate}

Week 2 represented a joint distribution with a DAG, where every edge has a direction. Some problems have no natural direction: neighbouring pixels in an image, for example, influence each other symmetrically. To see what directed edges cost us in such a problem, we look at how much of the graph a single variable depends on, which is measured by its Markov blanket.

Recall the **Markov blanket** of a variable $X_i$: the smallest set of other variables that makes $X_i$ conditionally independent of everything else. In a DAG, the Markov blanket of $X_i$ is its parents, its children, and its children's other parents (the co-parents), because of the explaining-away effect from Week 2 (@sec-cistructures in Week 2): observing a child can create dependence between that child's parents.

This has an awkward consequence. Take a grid of variables $X_1,\dots,X_{20}$ arranged in rows, where intuitively each variable should depend only on its four grid neighbors (up, down, left, right). If we try to encode this as a DAG by choosing some ordering of the variables (say, left to right, top to bottom) and drawing arrows accordingly, the Markov blanket of an interior node like $X_8$ can end up including nodes that have nothing to do with $X_8$'s grid neighbors. Figure 1 shows the lecture's version: every horizontal edge points right and every vertical edge points down.

Reading $X_8$'s Markov blanket off Figure 1 with the parents, children, co-parents rule:

- **Parents:** $X_3$ (above) and $X_7$ (left).
- **Children:** $X_9$ (right) and $X_{13}$ (below).
- **Co-parents:** the other parents of those children. $X_9$ has parents $X_4$ and $X_8$, so $X_4$ is a co-parent. $X_{13}$ has parents $X_8$ and $X_{12}$, so $X_{12}$ is a co-parent.

The first two groups are exactly $X_8$'s four grid neighbors, as we would expect. $X_4$ and $X_{12}$ are the surprise: they sit diagonally from $X_8$ and share no edge with it. They are in the blanket because of the **co-parent rule**, which comes from the **collider** case of Week 2's d-separation rule (@sec-bayesball in Week 2). The path $X_8\to X_9\leftarrow X_4$ meets head-to-head at $X_9$, so $X_9$ is a collider on it. A Markov blanket must contain $X_8$'s children, so $X_9$ is conditioned on. A collider blocks a path only when neither it nor any of its descendants is observed, so an observed collider leaves the path active. This is explaining away: given $X_9$, learning $X_4$ changes what we believe about $X_8$, its other cause. The only way to cut that path is to condition on $X_4$ too. The same argument through $X_{13}$ puts $X_{12}$ in the blanket.

The asymmetry gives the orientation away. The other two diagonal cells, $X_2$ and $X_{14}$, are not in the blanket: $X_2$'s children are $X_3$ and $X_7$, which are parents of $X_8$ rather than children, and $X_{14}$ is a child of $X_9$ and $X_{13}$, not a parent of either. Which diagonals join the blanket depends only on which way the arrows were drawn. The DAG is not wrong: it does encode a valid factorization. But its dependency structure does not match the "each cell depends on its neighbors" structure we actually wanted to express, and no choice of edge directions fixes this in general.

**Figure 1.** The lecture's grid as a DAG, with every edge pointing right or down. $X_8$'s Markov blanket is its parents $X_3, X_7$ (blue), its children $X_9, X_{13}$ (green), and its co-parents $X_4, X_{12}$ (orange). The highlighted edges $X_4\to X_9$ and $X_{12}\to X_{13}$ are what make $X_4$ and $X_{12}$ co-parents, even though neither is a grid neighbor of $X_8$.

## Markov random fields, cliques, and the factorization theorem {#sec-mrf}

The grid shows the problem with arrows: they force us to choose directions the problem does not have, and that choice drags non-neighbours like $X_4$ and $X_{12}$ into $X_8$'s blanket through colliders. The fix is to drop the arrows. In an undirected graph an edge only says "these two variables interact", there are no colliders, and (as @sec-hc will show) a node's Markov blanket is just its neighbours. An undirected graph then needs its own rule for which distributions it represents, which is what this section sets up.

::: {.definition-block}
**Definition.** An **undirected graphical model**, or **Markov random field (MRF)**, represents a set of random variables as nodes of an undirected graph $G$, where an edge between two nodes means those variables interact directly, rather than one causing the other.
:::

To write down what distributions an MRF represents, we need the notion of a clique.

::: {.definition-block}
**Definition.** A **clique** is a subset of nodes in which every pair is connected by an edge. A **maximal clique** is a clique that cannot be extended by adding one more adjacent node without breaking the all-pairs-connected property.
:::

::: {.definition-block}
**Definition.** Let $\boldsymbol{x} = (x_1,\dots,x_m)$ be all the variables in graph $G$, and let $\mathcal{C}$ be the set of all maximal cliques of $G$. A distribution $p$ **factorizes with respect to** $G$ if
$$p(\boldsymbol{x}) \propto \prod_{C \in \mathcal{C}} \psi_C(x_C)$$
for some nonnegative **potential functions** $\psi_C$, where $x_C = (x_i)_{i \in C}$. The MRF on $G$ represents exactly the distributions that factorize with respect to $G$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" .clarification title="Question: What does the C in psi_C mean, and are we free to define these functions however we like?"}
**What $C$ stands for.** $C$ is a clique: a set of node indices, such as $C=\{1,2,3\}$. The product $\prod_{C\in\mathcal{C}}$ runs over every maximal clique of the graph, and $x_C$ is the list of values of just the variables in that clique. So $\psi_C(x_C)$ is "the potential attached to clique $C$, evaluated at that clique's variables." In practice we write the clique's members as the subscript: for $C=\{1,2,3\}$, $\psi_C(x_C)$ is written $\psi_{1,2,3}(x_1,x_2,x_3)$. The letter $\psi$ (psi) has no meaning of its own; it is the usual name for a potential.

**What we may choose.** Almost anything, within three rules:

- **Nonnegative.** $\psi_C(x_C)\ge 0$ for every setting. Hammersley-Clifford (@sec-hc) needs the resulting $p$ to be strictly positive, which is why potentials are often written as $\psi_C = e^{(\text{something})}$, which can never be zero.
- **Only the clique's own variables.** $\psi_{1,2,3}$ may look at $x_1,x_2,x_3$ and nothing else. This rule is the entire content of the graph: it is what stops a factor from linking two variables that share no edge.
- **No normalization.** A potential need not sum to 1 and is not a probability. Multiplying one potential by a constant changes nothing once we divide by $Z$.

Within those rules, choosing the potentials is the modelling step. They are usually given a parametric form and learned from data, such as the Ising model's $\psi_{st}=e^{J_{st}x_sx_t}$ (@sec-ising) or the log-linear form of @sec-mrf-expfam.

**Potentials on smaller cliques.** We may also attach potentials to single nodes or to edges inside a larger clique, as the Ising model does with its per-node field. This does not enlarge the family of distributions: any such factor can be multiplied into the potential of a maximal clique that contains it, which recovers the one-potential-per-maximal-clique form above.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" .clarification title="Question: What does it mean for a distribution to factorize with respect to a graph, concretely?"}
**What "factorizes" means.** A function of many variables *factorizes* if it can be written as a product of smaller functions, each of which looks at only some of the variables. Week 2 already did this for DAGs: $p(x_1,\dots,x_N)=\prod_ip(x_i\mid\text{parents}(x_i))$, where each factor involves one node and its parents (@sec-dag in Week 2). Here the factors are potentials instead of conditional probabilities, and the graph decides which groups of variables are allowed to share a factor: one factor per maximal clique. "With respect to $G$" means exactly that restriction. Any distribution can be written as a single factor over all its variables, but that only factorizes with respect to the complete graph.

**A concrete example.** Take the chain $X_1-X_2-X_3$ with each $X_i\in\{0,1\}$. Its maximal cliques are the edges $\{1,2\}$ and $\{2,3\}$, so a distribution factorizes with respect to this graph if
$$p(x_1,x_2,x_3)=\frac1Z\,\psi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2)\,\psi_{2,3}(x_2,x_3).$$
Choose both potentials to reward agreement, as in the Ising model of @sec-ising: $\psi(a,b)=2$ if $a=b$ and $1$ if $a\neq b$. Multiplying the two potentials for each of the 8 settings gives the unnormalized table:

| $(x_1,x_2,x_3)$ | 000 | 001 | 010 | 011 | 100 | 101 | 110 | 111 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\psi_{1,2}\,\psi_{2,3}$ | 4 | 2 | 1 | 2 | 2 | 1 | 2 | 4 |

The entries sum to $Z=18$, so for example $p(0,0,0)=4/18=2/9$ and $p(0,1,0)=1/18$. Eight probabilities were specified by two $2\times2$ tables: that saving is the point of factorizing.

**What the factorization buys.** Because no factor contains both $x_1$ and $x_3$, they can only influence each other through $x_2$. Check it with the definition of conditional probability (Bayes' rule), dividing the joint by the marginal of what we condition on:
$$p(x_3\mid x_1,x_2)=\frac{p(x_1,x_2,x_3)}{p(x_1,x_2)}=\frac{p(x_1,x_2,x_3)}{\sum_{x_3'}p(x_1,x_2,x_3')}.$$
The $\frac1Z$ in every joint probability cancels between numerator and denominator, so the table entries can be used directly. With $x_2=0$ and $x_1=0$:
$$p(x_3=0\mid x_1=0,x_2=0)=\frac{p(0,0,0)}{p(0,0,0)+p(0,0,1)}=\frac{4/18}{4/18+2/18}=\frac{4}{4+2}=\frac23.$$
With $x_2=0$ and $x_1=1$:
$$p(x_3=0\mid x_1=1,x_2=0)=\frac{p(1,0,0)}{p(1,0,0)+p(1,0,1)}=\frac{2/18}{2/18+1/18}=\frac{2}{2+1}=\frac23.$$
Changing $x_1$ does not change the answer once $x_2$ is known, so $X_1\perp X_3\mid X_2$. This is the independence that @sec-hc reads directly off the graph.

**A distribution that does not factorize.** Let $X_2$ be a fair coin, independent of everything, and let $X_1=X_3$ be a second fair coin, so $p(x_1,x_2,x_3)=\frac14$ when $x_1=x_3$ and $0$ otherwise. Given $x_2$, knowing $x_1$ still tells us $x_3$ exactly, so $X_1\not\perp X_3\mid X_2$. Every distribution of the form $\frac1Z\psi_{1,2}\psi_{2,3}$ has $X_1\perp X_3\mid X_2$ (the general proof is the chain argument in @sec-hc; the check above is one instance), so no choice of potentials can produce this one. It factorizes only with respect to a graph with an edge between $X_1$ and $X_3$.
:::

Unlike a DAG's conditional probability tables, a potential $\psi_C$ need not sum or integrate to 1, and need not have any probabilistic interpretation on its own; it is simply a nonnegative score attached to each joint setting of the clique's variables. The product of all the potentials is only proportional to $p(\boldsymbol{x})$, so an explicit normalizing constant $Z = \sum_{\boldsymbol{x}} \prod_{C} \psi_C(x_C)$ (the **partition function**) is needed to turn it into an actual probability. This factored structure is what makes sums and integrals over $p(\boldsymbol{x})$ tractable: instead of manipulating one giant table over all variables jointly, we manipulate several small tables, one per clique, exactly the same motivation that drove the chain-rule factorization of Week 2 (@sec-factoring in Week 2).

As a small concrete instance, a 4-cycle of binary variables $x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4$ (edges $1\text{-}2$, $2\text{-}3$, $3\text{-}4$, $4\text{-}1$) has four maximal cliques, one per edge, so

$$p(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4) = \frac{1}{Z}\,\psi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2)\,\psi_{2,3}(x_2,x_3)\,\psi_{3,4}(x_3,x_4)\,\psi_{1,4}(x_1,x_4).$$

**Figure 2.** A 4-cycle: each edge is its own maximal clique, since no three nodes here are all pairwise connected. Each $\psi$ can be stored as a small table (for binary variables, 4 numbers per edge); these numbers are potentials, not probabilities, since the normalizer $Z$ has not been applied.

Because the variables are finite discrete, each potential really is just a table of nonnegative numbers. The lecture gives these four tables for the 4-cycle. Each row is one setting of the edge's two variables, listed in the order the potential takes them (for $\psi_{1,4}$, that is $(x_1,x_4)$):

| Setting of the edge | $\psi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2)$ | $\psi_{2,3}(x_2,x_3)$ | $\psi_{3,4}(x_3,x_4)$ | $\psi_{1,4}(x_1,x_4)$ |
|:---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| $(0,0)$ | 30 | 100 | 1 | 100 |
| $(0,1)$ | 5 | 1 | 100 | 1 |
| $(1,0)$ | 1 | 1 | 100 | 1 |
| $(1,1)$ | 10 | 100 | 1 | 100 |

A larger entry makes that setting of the pair more likely, other things equal. So $\psi_{2,3}$ and $\psi_{1,4}$ strongly favour their two variables agreeing, $\psi_{3,4}$ strongly favours $x_3$ and $x_4$ disagreeing, and $\psi_{1,2}$ mildly favours $(0,0)$. None of the columns sums to 1. To get the probability of one full setting, multiply the four matching entries, then divide by $Z$, the sum of those products over all $2^4=16$ settings.

## The Hammersley-Clifford theorem {#sec-hc}

We now have two ways to read an undirected graph. @sec-mrf reads it as a **factorization**: a product of clique potentials. The motivation in @sec-motivate reads it as a set of **independence statements**: a variable should depend only on its neighbours. Nothing so far says these two readings describe the same distributions. The Hammersley-Clifford theorem says they do, for distributions that are strictly positive.

::: {.theorem-block}
**Hammersley-Clifford theorem.** If $p(\boldsymbol{x}) > 0$ for all $\boldsymbol{x}$, the following are equivalent:

- $p$ factorizes with respect to $G$, i.e. $p(\boldsymbol{x}) \propto \prod_{C \in \mathcal{C}} \psi_C(x_C)$ for nonnegative potentials $\psi_C$.
- **Global Markov property:** $X_A \perp X_B \mid X_S$ whenever $S$ separates $A$ from $B$ in $G$ (every path from $A$ to $B$ passes through $S$).
:::

Two special cases of the global Markov property are worth naming directly, since they recur constantly: if $i$ and $j$ are not joined by an edge, then $X_i \perp X_j \mid X_{\text{rest}}$ (conditioning on every other variable separates any two non-adjacent nodes); and the Markov blanket of $X_i$ in an MRF is simply its graph neighbors, no co-parent correction needed, in contrast to the DAG case of @sec-motivate.

**Why the two directions match: a chain.** The core mechanism is easiest to see on a three-node chain $X-Y-Z$, whose only maximal cliques are the edges $\{X,Y\}$ and $\{Y,Z\}$, so the class of distributions that factorizes with respect to this graph is exactly those of the form
$$f(x,y,z) = \alpha(x,y)\,\beta(y,z)$$
for positive functions $\alpha,\beta$. The claim is that this is equivalent to $X \perp Z \mid Y$.

*Independent $\Rightarrow$ factorized.* Using the product rule, $f(x,y,z) = f(y,z)\,f(x\mid y,z)$, and separately $f(x,y,z) = f(x\mid y)\,f(y,z)$ whenever $X\perp Z\mid Y$ already holds, so a factorization of the stated form is available with $\alpha(x,y) = f(x\mid y)$ and $\beta(y,z) = f(y,z)$. This direction just restates the definition of conditional independence as a factorization.

*Factorized $\Rightarrow$ independent, without assuming it first.* Start only from $f(x,y,z)=\alpha(x,y)\beta(y,z)$ and derive the independence. Summing out $x$,
$$f(y,z) = \Big(\sum_x \alpha(x,y)\Big)\beta(y,z).$$
Dividing the joint by this marginal gives the conditional:
$$f(x\mid y,z) = \frac{\alpha(x,y)\,\beta(y,z)}{\left(\sum_x \alpha(x,y)\right)\beta(y,z)} = \frac{\alpha(x,y)}{\sum_x \alpha(x,y)}.$$
The right-hand side has no $z$ in it at all, so $f(x\mid y,z)$ does not depend on $z$, which is exactly $X\perp Z\mid Y$. The mechanism is the same cancellation as Week 2's causal-chain check (@sec-cistructures in Week 2): a shared factor in numerator and denominator drops out, leaving no trace of the conditioned-out variable.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" .clarification title="Question: If no potential contains both x and z, are X and Z independent even when Y is not observed?"}
No. The factorization gives independence only *given* $Y$. Without $Y$, the two ends of the chain are generally dependent, because each one carries information about $Y$, and $Y$ carries information about the other.

Take binary $x,y,z$ and the agreement potentials from the factorization example in @sec-mrf: $\alpha(x,y)=2$ if $x=y$ and $1$ otherwise, and $\beta(y,z)$ defined the same way. The eight products $\alpha\beta$ sum to $18$.

**Given $Y$, independent.** At $y=1$, the four products are $4$ (for $x=z=1$), $2$, $2$, and $1$, summing to $9$. So
$$P(X=1,Z=1\mid Y=1)=\frac49=\frac23\cdot\frac23=P(X=1\mid Y=1)\,P(Z=1\mid Y=1).$$

**Without $Y$, dependent.** By symmetry $P(X=1)=P(Z=1)=\tfrac12$, so independence would need $P(X=1,Z=1)=\tfrac14=\tfrac{4.5}{18}$. Summing over $y$ instead:
$$P(X=1,Z=1)=\frac{\alpha(1,0)\,\beta(0,1)+\alpha(1,1)\,\beta(1,1)}{18}=\frac{1+4}{18}=\frac{5}{18}.$$
Since $\tfrac{5}{18}\neq\tfrac{4.5}{18}$, $X$ and $Z$ are dependent.

**Why the split breaks.** Each term of $\sum_y\alpha(x,y)\,\beta(y,z)$ is a function of $x$ times a function of $z$, but a sum of two such products is generally not itself a product. Observing $Y$ picks out a single term, and that term does split. This is the Ising practice question of @sec-ising worked in numbers, and the same pattern as the causal chain of @sec-cistructures in Week 2.
:::

## Worked example: cliques, factorization, and independence {#sec-mrf-example}

With both readings in hand, we apply them to one graph: find its maximal cliques, write the factorization they give, then read independencies off the graph by separation, which Hammersley-Clifford guarantees will agree with the factorization.

**Figure 3.** A seven-node MRF with edges $1\text{-}2, 1\text{-}3, 2\text{-}3, 2\text{-}4, 2\text{-}5, 3\text{-}5, 3\text{-}6, 4\text{-}5, 4\text{-}6, 4\text{-}7, 5\text{-}6, 5\text{-}7, 6\text{-}7$.

**How many maximal cliques are there?** Checking every pairwise connection within each candidate set gives five maximal cliques: $\{1,2,3\}$, $\{2,3,5\}$, $\{2,4,5\}$, $\{3,5,6\}$, and $\{4,5,6,7\}$. Node 5 belongs to four of the five, since it connects to nearly every other node; that is exactly why it appears in so many of the clique's variable lists below.

**What is the factorization?**
$$p(\boldsymbol{x}) \propto \psi_{1,2,3}(x_1,x_2,x_3)\,\psi_{2,3,5}(x_2,x_3,x_5)\,\psi_{2,4,5}(x_2,x_4,x_5)$$
$${}\times \psi_{3,5,6}(x_3,x_5,x_6)\,\psi_{4,5,6,7}(x_4,x_5,x_6,x_7).$$

**What independencies does the graph imply?** Reading the global Markov property off the picture: removing $\{3,4,5\}$ disconnects $\{1,2\}$ from $\{6,7\}$ entirely (every path from $1$ or $2$ to $6$ or $7$ passes through $3$, $4$, or $5$), so $(X_1,X_2) \perp (X_6,X_7) \mid (X_3,X_4,X_5)$. Similarly, every path from $1$ to $5$ passes through $2$ or $3$, so $X_1 \perp X_5 \mid (X_2,X_3)$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" .clarification title="Question: How does the factorization itself prove these independencies, not just the picture?"}
Hammersley-Clifford promises that separation and factorization agree. We can check this directly for $(X_1,X_2)\perp(X_6,X_7)\mid(X_3,X_4,X_5)$, with $A=\{1,2\}$, $B=\{6,7\}$, $S=\{3,4,5\}$.

**No clique touches both sides.** The pairs 1-6, 1-7, 2-6, 2-7 are all non-edges, and a clique needs every pair joined, so no clique holds a node of $A$ and a node of $B$. Each clique lies inside $A\cup S$ or inside $B\cup S$:

| Side | Cliques |
|---|---|
| inside $A\cup S$ | $\{1,2,3\}$, $\{2,3,5\}$, $\{2,4,5\}$ |
| inside $B\cup S$ | $\{3,5,6\}$, $\{4,5,6,7\}$ |

**Group the factors by side.**
$$p(\boldsymbol x)=\frac1Z\,f(x_A,x_S)\,g(x_B,x_S),$$
$$f=\psi_{1,2,3}\,\psi_{2,3,5}\,\psi_{2,4,5},\qquad g=\psi_{3,5,6}\,\psi_{4,5,6,7}.$$

**Condition on $x_S$.** Dividing by $p(x_S)$, the $\frac1Z$ cancels. In the denominator, $g$ does not depend on $x_A'$, so the distributive law splits the double sum into a product of two single sums:
$$\begin{aligned}
p(x_A,x_B\mid x_S)&=\frac{f(x_A,x_S)\,g(x_B,x_S)}{\sum_{x_A'}\sum_{x_B'}f(x_A',x_S)\,g(x_B',x_S)}\\
&=\frac{f(x_A,x_S)}{\sum_{x_A'}f(x_A',x_S)}\cdot\frac{g(x_B,x_S)}{\sum_{x_B'}g(x_B',x_S)}.
\end{aligned}$$
Each fraction sums to 1 over its own variables, so summing over $x_B$ shows the first is $p(x_A\mid x_S)$, and summing over $x_A$ shows the second is $p(x_B\mid x_S)$. That is the definition of conditional independence.

**Nodes that are neither observed nor in the claim.** For $X_1\perp X_6\mid(X_2,X_3)$, nodes 4, 5, 7 stay random and are summed out. Only $\psi_{1,2,3}$ lacks all of $x_4,x_5,x_7$, so it moves outside the sums:
$$p(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_6)=\frac1Z\,\psi_{1,2,3}(x_1,x_2,x_3)\,\tilde g(x_2,x_3,x_6),$$
where $\tilde g=\sum_{x_4,x_5,x_7}\psi_{2,3,5}\,\psi_{2,4,5}\,\psi_{3,5,6}\,\psi_{4,5,6,7}$ is left depending only on $x_2,x_3,x_6$. This is again a function of $(x_1,x_S)$ times a function of $(x_6,x_S)$, so the same conditioning step applies.

**When it fails.** Try $X_2\perp X_6\mid(X_4,X_5)$. Node 3 is unobserved, $\psi_{2,3,5}$ contains $x_2$ and $x_3$, and $\psi_{3,5,6}$ contains $x_3$ and $x_6$. Summing out $x_3$ leaves one factor containing both $x_2$ and $x_6$, so no split exists. In the graph, this is the path 2-3-6, which avoids $\{4,5\}$.

The general check: cross the observed variables out of every factor, join two remaining variables whenever some factor contains both, and see whether any chain of joins links $A$ to $B$. This is graph separation stated in terms of factors.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
**Practice question.** In Figure 3, is $X_1 \perp X_4 \mid X_2$? Check by finding every path from node 1 to node 4 and seeing whether $\{2\}$ blocks all of them.

**Solution.** Node 1's only edges go to nodes 2 and 3, so every path out of node 1 starts by visiting 2 or 3. A path starting $1\to 2 \to 4$ is blocked once we condition on $\{2\}$, since 2 is on that path and is now fixed. But a path starting $1\to 3 \to 5 \to 4$ never touches node 2 at all, so conditioning on $\{2\}$ does nothing to it: it stays open. Since at least one path from 1 to 4 survives, $\{2\}$ does not separate them, so $X_1 \not\perp X_4 \mid X_2$. Separating 1 from 4 would require conditioning on a set that intersects every route out of node 1's second neighbor, node 3, as well, for example $\{2,3\}$ or $\{2,5,6\}$.
:::

## What MRFs can express that DAGs cannot, and vice versa {#sec-mrf-vs-dag}

The grid made MRFs look like a strict improvement on DAGs. They are not: the two representations are not nested, and each can express independence patterns the other cannot.

**An MRF with no equivalent DAG.** Take the 4-cycle $A-D-C-B-A$ shown below (edges $A\text{-}D$, $A\text{-}B$, $D\text{-}C$, $B\text{-}C$, and *no* diagonal). Its two non-adjacent pairs give two independence statements simultaneously: $A \perp C \mid \{D,B\}$ and $B \perp D \mid \{A,C\}$. Any attempt to encode this as a DAG by orienting the four edges necessarily creates a v-structure (a collider) at one of the four nodes, and by the explaining-away logic of Week 2, that collider blocks one of the two independencies while leaving the other intact, or introduces an independence (such as making $B$ and $D$ marginally independent) that was never true in the undirected model. No orientation of the diamond's edges reproduces both independencies at once.

**Figure 4.** A diamond MRF. Both $A\perp C\mid\{D,B\}$ and $B\perp D\mid\{A,C\}$ hold simultaneously; no directed version of this graph reproduces both.

**A DAG with no equivalent MRF.** Conversely, take the explaining-away structure from Week 2, $X \to Z \leftarrow Y$. There, $X$ and $Y$ are marginally independent ($X\perp Y$) but become dependent once $Z$ is observed ($X \not\perp Y \mid Z$). An undirected model cannot express this pattern: the global Markov property says that if $X \perp Y$ holds unconditionally, no set of nodes we condition on can ever *create* a dependency between them, since observing more variables in an MRF can only add to the separating set, never remove an edge. Collider-created dependence is a genuinely directed phenomenon.

## MRFs as exponential families {#sec-mrf-expfam}

So far a potential has been any nonnegative table, and the graph has told us only which variables share a potential. To learn potentials from data we need a parameterized family. Week 1 already gave us one with a complete MLE theory, the exponential family, and this section shows that MRFs fit into it.

::: {.callout-note}
**Homework-relevant.** This section's log-linear form and sufficient statistics are the same exponential-family machinery from Week 1 (@sec-mle in Week 1), applied to potentials instead of a single density. If a current or upcoming assignment asks you to write an MRF or a Gaussian graphical model in exponential-family form, this derivation pattern is the one to reuse.
:::

Consider the parametric family
$$p(\boldsymbol{x}\mid\theta) = \frac{1}{Z(\theta)}\prod_{C\in\mathcal{C}} \psi_C(x_C\mid\theta_C), \qquad \theta = (\theta_C)_{C\in\mathcal{C}}.$$
Taking the log of the product turns it into a sum, exactly as in Week 1's move from likelihood to log-likelihood:
$$p(\boldsymbol{x}\mid\theta) = \exp\Big\{\sum_{C\in\mathcal{C}} \log\psi_C(x_C\mid\theta_C) - \underbrace{\log Z(\theta)}_{=A(\theta)}\Big\}.$$
If each potential has a **log-linear form**, $\log\psi_C(x_C\mid\theta_C) = \theta_C^\top \phi_C(x_C)$, this becomes exactly Week 1's exponential family, with natural parameter $\theta$, sufficient statistic $\phi = (\phi_C)_{C\in\mathcal{C}}$, and log-partition function $A(\theta) = \log Z(\theta)$:
$$p(\boldsymbol{x}\mid\theta) = \exp\Big\{\sum_{C\in\mathcal{C}} \theta_C^\top \phi_C(x_C) - A(\theta)\Big\}.$$

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" .clarification title="Question: Where does the log-linear form come from, and why do we want an exponential family at all?"}
**The core idea.** We choose the potentials so that the *log* of each one is a weighted sum of features of its clique's variables:
$$\log\psi_C(x_C\mid\theta_C) = \theta_C^\top\phi_C(x_C) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \psi_C(x_C\mid\theta_C) = \exp\{\theta_C^\top\phi_C(x_C)\}.$$
So $\psi_C$ is not $\theta$ times a function of $x$. Its log is, and $\psi_C$ is the exponential of that (which also keeps it positive). This is a modelling choice, not something derived from the MRF definition. We make it because it is exactly what Week 1's template needs.

**What each object is.** For a clique $C$ with $|C|$ variables and $d_C$ chosen features:

| Object | Input | Output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $x_C$ | (none) | the values of the clique's $\lvert C\rvert$ variables, e.g. $(x_1,x_2)\in\{0,1\}^2$ |
| $\phi_C$ (feature map) | $x_C$ | a vector in $\mathbb{R}^{d_C}$ |
| $\theta_C$ (weights) | (none) | a vector in $\mathbb{R}^{d_C}$, one weight per feature |
| $\psi_C$ (potential) | $x_C$ | a positive number |
| $\log\psi_C$ | $x_C$ | a real number |

**Why the transpose.** Both $\theta_C$ and $\phi_C(x_C)$ are column vectors of length $d_C$. $\log\psi_C$ must be a single number, and $\theta_C^\top\phi_C(x_C)$, a $(1\times d_C)$ row times a $(d_C\times 1)$ column, is the dot product $\sum_{k=1}^{d_C}\theta_{C,k}\,\phi_{C,k}(x_C)$: each feature times its own weight, summed. Without the transpose, $\theta_C\phi_C$ would be a column times a column, which is undefined.

**Why this makes an exponential family.** Run Week 1's recipe (@sec-expfam):

- $\log Z(\theta)$ sums over all $\boldsymbol x$, so it depends only on $\theta$. It plays the role of $A(\theta)$.
- Each $\log\psi_C$ mixes data and parameters, so it must factor as (parameters)$^\top$(function of data). The log-linear form is precisely that requirement, clique by clique. A potential like $\psi_C = 1+\theta_C x_C$ fails, since $\log(1+\theta_C x_C)$ does not split.
- A sum of dot products is one dot product of stacked vectors. With $\theta\in\mathbb{R}^d$ and $\phi(\boldsymbol x)\in\mathbb{R}^d$ the concatenations over cliques, $d=\sum_C d_C$:
$$\sum_C\theta_C^\top\phi_C(x_C) = \theta^\top\phi(\boldsymbol x).$$

This gives natural parameter $\theta$, sufficient statistic $\phi$, $h=1$, and $A(\theta)=\log Z(\theta)$, a map from $\mathbb{R}^d$ to $\mathbb{R}$.

**Examples.** The Ising model (@sec-ising) has $d_{st}=1$: $\phi_{st}=x_sx_t$ and $\theta_{st}=J_{st}$. For a discrete table, indicator features always work. A binary edge with invented values $\psi(0,0)=2$, $\psi(0,1)=1$, $\psi(1,0)=1$, $\psi(1,1)=4$ has $d_C=4$, $\theta_C=(\log 2,0,0,\log 4)$, and $\phi_C(1,1)=(0,0,0,1)$, so $\theta_C^\top\phi_C(1,1)=\log 4$.

**Why we want this.** From Week 1:

- the data enter only through $\sum_n\phi(\boldsymbol x^{(n)})$ (clique counts, for indicator features);
- $\nabla A(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_\theta[\phi(\boldsymbol X)]$ (@sec-mean), so the MLE matches the model's clique marginals to the data's clique frequencies;
- the second derivative of $A$ is a covariance, so $A$ is convex and the log-likelihood is concave, with no spurious local maxima.

The catch is that $Z$ and its gradient sum over every joint configuration, which is why inference keeps returning in later weeks.
:::

**When does the log-linear form hold?** For finite discrete $x_C$, $\log\psi_C$ takes only finitely many values, one per setting of $x_C$. Let $\theta_C$ list all those values, and let $\phi_C(x_C)$ be the indicator vector with a 1 in the entry matching $x_C$'s current setting and 0 elsewhere: then $\theta_C^\top \phi_C(x_C)$ just selects out the one matching entry, which is $\log\psi_C(x_C\mid\theta_C)$ by construction. As in Week 1's exponential-family facts, the log-partition function's gradient recovers an expectation: $\partial \log Z(\theta) / \partial \theta_C = \mathbb{E}[\phi_C(X_C)]$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" .clarification title="Question: What does the paragraph on the log-linear form mean in plain terms?"}
In plain terms, the paragraph says that for a small group of variables with only finitely many settings, any table of positive numbers over those settings can be written as the exponential of a weighted sum. For finite discrete groups this form is always available, so using it costs nothing.

**Step 1: the table becomes a list of weights.** Suppose a group of variables $x_C$ has finitely many settings, for example two binary variables with four settings in total. Its potential $\psi_C$ gives one positive number per setting. Take the log of each number and stack the results into a list $\theta_C$. That gives one weight per setting.

**Step 2: a 0/1 vector picks out the right weight.** For the setting that currently holds, build the vector $\phi_C(x_C)$ that is all zeros except for a single 1 in that setting's slot. Taking the dot product of $\theta_C$ with this vector keeps only the weight in the slot marked 1. That weight is the log of the potential at the current setting, so the weighted sum reproduces the original table exactly.

**Step 3: the slope of the normalizing sum gives probabilities.** $\log Z(\theta)$ is the log of the sum over every joint setting of all the variables. Its slope with respect to one group's weights is the model's average value of that group's 0/1 vector. Each entry of that average is the probability that the group sits in the matching setting, so the slope for a weight is the probability of its setting.

Put simply, this section is a relabeling. A table of log-values is written as a dot product with a 0/1 vector, and the exponential-family tools from Week 1 then apply to it.
:::

**Worked example: minimal vs. non-minimal.** We now run the finite-discrete construction on the smallest MRF where it is interesting, following the tutorial. The goal is to see exactly what $\theta$ and $\phi$ look like, check that they rebuild the potentials, and find the one parameter per edge that this construction wastes.

**Step 1: the model.**
$$X_1 - X_2 - X_3, \qquad x_1, x_2, x_3 \in \{0,1\}$$
$$p(x_1,x_2,x_3\mid\theta) = \frac{1}{Z(\theta)}\,\psi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2\mid\theta_{1,2})\,\psi_{2,3}(x_2,x_3\mid\theta_{2,3})$$
The chain has two maximal cliques, the edges $\{1,2\}$ and $\{2,3\}$, so by Hammersley-Clifford the distribution is one potential per edge, multiplied and normalized. At this point $\psi_{1,2}$ is only a positive function of two binary variables. Two binary variables have four joint settings, so $\psi_{1,2}$ is nothing more than a table of four positive numbers, and the same holds for $\psi_{2,3}$. We have not yet said how $\theta$ controls those tables; Steps 3 to 5 do that.

**Step 2: move everything into one exponent.**
$$p(x_1,x_2,x_3\mid\theta) = \exp\big\{\log\psi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2\mid\theta_{1,2}) + \log\psi_{2,3}(x_2,x_3\mid\theta_{2,3}) - \log Z(\theta)\big\}$$
This is the same distribution, rewritten using $a = e^{\log a}$. We do it because Week 1's exponential family has the shape $\exp\{\theta^\top\phi(\boldsymbol x) - A(\theta)\}$: one exponent, made of a dot product minus a term that depends only on $\theta$. Taking logs turns the product of potentials into a sum. So if each $\log\psi$ can be written as a dot product, the whole exponent becomes one dot product, and the model is an exponential family.

**Step 3: define the weights $\theta_{1,2}$.**
$$\theta_{1,2} := \begin{bmatrix}\log\psi_{1,2}(0,0)\\ \log\psi_{1,2}(0,1)\\ \log\psi_{1,2}(1,0)\\ \log\psi_{1,2}(1,1)\end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^4$$
$\log\psi_{1,2}$ takes exactly four values, one per setting, and those four values are what we would learn from data. Calling the list of them $\theta_{1,2}$ makes the unknowns of the model its parameters directly, with nothing hidden. The order $(0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)$ is a bookkeeping choice, but it has to be the same order that $\phi_{1,2}$ uses in Step 4.

**Step 4: define the features $\phi_{1,2}$.**
$$\phi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2) := \begin{bmatrix}(1-x_1)(1-x_2)\\ (1-x_1)\,x_2\\ x_1\,(1-x_2)\\ x_1\,x_2\end{bmatrix}$$
Each entry is a product that equals 1 for exactly one setting and 0 for the other three. For example, $(1-x_1)\,x_2$ is 1 only when $x_1=0$ and $x_2=1$. Plugging in the four settings gives the four indicator vectors:
$$\phi_{1,2}(0,0)=\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\\0\\0\end{bmatrix},\quad \phi_{1,2}(0,1)=\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\\0\\0\end{bmatrix},$$
$$\phi_{1,2}(1,0)=\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\\1\\0\end{bmatrix},\quad \phi_{1,2}(1,1)=\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\\0\\1\end{bmatrix}$$
We want a vector with a single 1 because Step 5 multiplies it against $\theta_{1,2}$, and a single 1 picks out a single weight. Writing the entries as products of $x_1$ and $x_2$, rather than as a lookup rule, gives one formula that holds for every setting at once. That formula is what lets us do algebra on $\phi$ in Step 8.

**Step 5: check the dot product, and define $\psi$ from it.** For the setting $(0,1)$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\theta_{1,2}^\top\phi_{1,2}(0,1) &= \log\psi_{1,2}(0,0)\cdot 0 + \log\psi_{1,2}(0,1)\cdot 1 \\
&\quad + \log\psi_{1,2}(1,0)\cdot 0 + \log\psi_{1,2}(1,1)\cdot 0 \\
&= \log\psi_{1,2}(0,1)
\end{aligned}
$$
The zeros in $\phi$ cancel every weight except the one for the current setting. The same happens for each of the four settings, so the dot product reproduces the whole table:
$$\log\psi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2\mid\theta_{1,2}) = \theta_{1,2}^\top\phi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2)$$
$$\Longleftrightarrow\quad \psi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2\mid\theta_{1,2}) := \exp\{\theta_{1,2}^\top\phi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2)\}$$
This is where $\psi$ is actually defined in this model. Step 3 built $\theta$ from the table, and this line turns that around: **any** $\theta_{1,2}\in\mathbb{R}^4$ now defines a potential table, by exponentiating the selected weight. The exponential keeps every entry positive, as an MRF potential must be, without constraining $\theta$. The tutorial phrases this as "let $\psi_{1,2}$ be the function that satisfies" the first equation. Repeating Steps 3 to 5 for the edge $\{2,3\}$ gives $\theta_{2,3}$ and $\phi_{2,3}(x_2,x_3)$, with $x_2,x_3$ in place of $x_1,x_2$.

**Step 6: read off the exponential family.** Substituting Step 5 into Step 2:
$$p(x_1,x_2,x_3\mid\theta) = \exp\big\{\theta_{1,2}^\top\phi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2) + \theta_{2,3}^\top\phi_{2,3}(x_2,x_3) - \log Z(\theta)\big\}$$
Matching this to Week 1's template, the natural parameter is $\theta = (\theta_{1,2},\theta_{2,3}) \in \mathbb{R}^8$, the sufficient statistic is $\phi = (\phi_{1,2},\phi_{2,3})$, and the log-partition function is $A(\theta)=\log Z(\theta)$, with
$$Z(\theta) = \sum_{\boldsymbol x\in\{0,1\}^3}\exp\big\{\theta_{1,2}^\top\phi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2) + \theta_{2,3}^\top\phi_{2,3}(x_2,x_3)\big\}.$$
The tutorial takes the potentials to be normalized already, meaning their product sums to 1 over all eight settings. Under that convention $Z(\theta)=1$.

**Step 7: why this representation is not minimal.**
$$\phi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2)^\top\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\\1\\1\end{bmatrix} = 1 \quad\text{for all } (x_1,x_2)\in\{0,1\}^2$$
Exactly one entry of $\phi_{1,2}$ is ever on, so its entries always sum to 1. All four possible values of $\phi_{1,2}$ therefore lie on the hyperplane $\{v : v^\top(1,1,1,1)^\top = 1\}$ rather than spreading through $\mathbb{R}^4$. An exponential family is **minimal** when no such fixed linear relation ties its sufficient statistics together, so this one is not.

The cost shows up as soon as we shift every weight by the same constant $c$:
$$(\theta_{1,2} + c\,\mathbf{1})^\top\phi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2) = \theta_{1,2}^\top\phi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2) + c$$
The shift adds $c$ to $\log\psi_{1,2}$ at every setting, which multiplies the whole table by $e^c$. Dividing by $Z$ cancels that factor, so two different parameter vectors give the same distribution. The four weights per edge carry only three numbers' worth of information about $p$.

The tutorial says that a non-minimal family fails the gradient identity $\nabla A(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_\theta[\phi(\boldsymbol X)]$ (@sec-mean). More precisely, the identity still holds for the true log-partition function $A(\theta)=\log Z(\theta)$. What fails is identifiability (different $\theta$ give the same distribution, as just shown, and $A$ is not strictly convex). The identity only appears to fail if $\theta$ is restricted to the set where $Z(\theta)=1$, because then $A=0$ there and the coordinates of $\theta$ cannot vary independently.

**Step 8: the fix, using $(0,0)$ as a reference.** Rearranging the hyperplane relation of Step 7 writes the first entry of $\phi_{1,2}$ in terms of the other three:
$$(1-x_1)(1-x_2) = 1 - (1-x_1)\,x_2 - x_1(1-x_2) - x_1x_2$$
Substituting this into $\theta_{1,2}^\top\phi_{1,2}$ and grouping by entry:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\log\psi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2) &= \log\psi_{1,2}(0,0) \\
&\quad + \big[\log\psi_{1,2}(0,1)-\log\psi_{1,2}(0,0)\big]\,(1-x_1)\,x_2 \\
&\quad + \big[\log\psi_{1,2}(1,0)-\log\psi_{1,2}(0,0)\big]\,x_1(1-x_2) \\
&\quad + \big[\log\psi_{1,2}(1,1)-\log\psi_{1,2}(0,0)\big]\,x_1x_2
\end{aligned}
$$
The first line does not depend on $x$, so it is a constant. The other three lines are again weights times features, which suggests the new parameters and statistics:
$$
\bar\theta_{1,2} := \begin{bmatrix}
\log\psi_{1,2}(0,1)-\log\psi_{1,2}(0,0)\\
\log\psi_{1,2}(1,0)-\log\psi_{1,2}(0,0)\\
\log\psi_{1,2}(1,1)-\log\psi_{1,2}(0,0)
\end{bmatrix}
$$
$$\bar\phi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2) := \begin{bmatrix}(1-x_1)\,x_2\\ x_1(1-x_2)\\ x_1x_2\end{bmatrix}$$
so that $\log\psi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2) = \log\psi_{1,2}(0,0) + \bar\theta_{1,2}^\top\bar\phi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2)$. Each new weight is a **contrast**: how much larger the log-potential is at that setting than at $(0,0)$. The reference setting has $\bar\phi_{1,2}(0,0) = \mathbf{0}$, so it needs no weight of its own. Adding the same $c$ to all four old weights leaves every contrast unchanged, which is exactly the redundancy of Step 7 removed. The vector $\bar\phi_{1,2}$ satisfies no fixed linear relation (its four possible values $\mathbf 0$, $e_1$, $e_2$, $e_3$ are not confined to any hyperplane), so each edge on its own is now minimal. The edge $\{2,3\}$ gets $\bar\theta_{2,3}$ and $\bar\phi_{2,3}(x_2,x_3)$ the same way.

**One redundancy is left across the two edges.** The edges share $x_2$, and their contrast features overlap through it:
$$(1-x_1)\,x_2 + x_1x_2 \;=\; x_2 \;=\; x_2(1-x_3) + x_2x_3 \qquad\text{for every } \boldsymbol x.$$
So adding $t$ to the first and third entries of $\bar\theta_{1,2}$ while subtracting $t$ from the second and third entries of $\bar\theta_{2,3}$ changes the exponent by $t\,x_2 - t\,x_2 = 0$, and the distribution does not move. The tutorial calls the six-parameter version minimal. That holds edge by edge, but not for the chain as a whole. Removing this last overlap leaves five statistics, $x_1, x_2, x_3, x_1x_2, x_2x_3$ (one weight per node and one per edge, the same shape as the Ising model in @sec-ising), and those five are minimal.

**Step 9: the new log-partition function.** Substituting into Step 2, the two constants $\log\psi_{1,2}(0,0)$ and $\log\psi_{2,3}(0,0)$ leave the data part of the exponent and join the normalizer:
$$p(x_1,x_2,x_3\mid\bar\theta) = \exp\big\{\bar\theta_{1,2}^\top\bar\phi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2) + \bar\theta_{2,3}^\top\bar\phi_{2,3}(x_2,x_3) - A(\bar\theta)\big\}$$
$$A(\bar\theta) = \log Z - \log\big(\psi_{1,2}(0,0)\,\psi_{2,3}(0,0)\big)$$
Under the $Z=1$ convention this is $A(\bar\theta) = -\log\big(\psi_{1,2}(0,0)\,\psi_{2,3}(0,0)\big)$. It is no longer identically zero. Because $p$ must sum to 1 over the eight settings, it can also be written purely in terms of $\bar\theta$, as the tutorial asks:
$$A(\bar\theta) = \log\sum_{\boldsymbol x\in\{0,1\}^3}\exp\big\{\bar\theta_{1,2}^\top\bar\phi_{1,2}(x_1,x_2) + \bar\theta_{2,3}^\top\bar\phi_{2,3}(x_2,x_3)\big\}$$
This is a genuine function of $\bar\theta$, not a constant, so the gradient identity can be used directly. Strict convexity needs one more step: $A$ is still flat along the cross-edge direction of Step 8, and only the five-statistic version removes that.

The general lesson: writing every table entry as its own parameter is always possible but wastes one degree of freedom per clique, because the normalizer erases each table's overall scale. Fixing a reference setting (here, $(0,0)$) and parameterizing only the *contrast* with it removes that waste inside each clique. When cliques share a variable, their contrasts can still overlap, and a fully minimal representation removes that overlap too.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" .clarification title="Question: What does it mean to write every table entry as its own parameter, and how does that waste a degree of freedom?"}
Take the potential $\psi_{1,2}$ from the 4-cycle tables at the end of @sec-mrf. Its table holds four numbers, one per setting of $(x_1,x_2)$: 30, 5, 1, 10. Writing every entry as its own parameter means the model stores all four as separate unknowns, here as their logs, $\theta_{1,2} = (\log 30, \log 5, \log 1, \log 10)$. Nothing ties one entry to another.

Now double every entry, to 60, 10, 2, 20. Each joint setting of the four variables uses exactly one entry of this table, so every product of potentials doubles. The normalizer $Z$ is the sum of those products, so it doubles too, and dividing by it cancels the factor. Every probability is exactly what it was before.

So the model cannot tell the two tables apart. What it actually responds to is how the entries compare with each other: setting $(0,0)$ scores 6 times setting $(0,1)$, 30 times setting $(1,0)$, and 3 times setting $(1,1)$. That is four numbers but only three comparisons. The fourth number only sets the overall size of the table, and the normalizer erases it.

That leftover number is the wasted **degree of freedom**: one parameter's worth of freedom that changes nothing about the distribution. Every clique's table has its own overall size, so the waste is one per clique.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" .clarification title="Question: What is a minimal representation?"}
A representation is the choice of features $\phi$ and weights $\theta$ used to write the model as $\exp\{\theta^\top\phi(\boldsymbol x) - A(\theta)\}$. It is **minimal** when no weight is spare: every change to $\theta$ changes the distribution, so each distribution has exactly one $\theta$.

The test is on the features. Suppose some fixed combination of the features always comes out to the same value, whatever $\boldsymbol x$ is. Then moving the weights along that combination shifts every exponent by the same amount, the normalizer cancels it, and the distribution does not change. The four indicator features of Step 7 always add up to 1, which is exactly this situation. A minimal representation has no such combination.

Why we care: with spare weights, many $\theta$ describe the same model. The best-fitting $\theta$ is then not unique, and the log-partition function $A$ is flat along the spare direction. With a minimal representation, each model has one parameter vector, and Week 1's facts (the gradient of $A$ is the expected features, and $A$ is strictly convex) apply cleanly.

Minimality is a property of the whole model, not of each table on its own. In the chain, each edge's contrasts are minimal by themselves, but the two edges share $x_2$ and still overlap in one direction (Step 8).
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" .clarification title="Question: What does it mean to fix a reference setting?"}
Only comparisons between entries of a table matter (see the first question above). So we pick one setting of the clique and describe every other setting by comparing it with that one. The chosen setting is the **reference**. In the worked example it is $(0,0)$, where both variables are 0. Any setting would work; $(0,0)$ is the tutorial's convention.

Fixing it means the reference setting gets no weight of its own. Its log-potential, $\log\psi_{1,2}(0,0)$, is a constant that does not depend on $\boldsymbol x$, so it leaves the data part of the exponent and joins the normalizer (Step 9). For the 4-cycle's $\psi_{1,2}$, the reference entry is 30, and every other entry is now described relative to 30.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" .clarification title="Question: What does it mean to parameterize only the contrast with the reference setting?"}
A **contrast** is a comparison between one setting and the reference. Here it is a difference of log-potentials, which is the log of a ratio:
$$\log\psi_{1,2}(0,1) - \log\psi_{1,2}(0,0) = \log\frac{\psi_{1,2}(0,1)}{\psi_{1,2}(0,0)}.$$
For the 4-cycle's $\psi_{1,2}$ (entries 30, 5, 1, 10) the three contrasts are
$$\log\tfrac{5}{30},\qquad \log\tfrac{1}{30},\qquad \log\tfrac{10}{30},$$
one for each setting other than the reference. A negative contrast means that setting is favoured less than the reference; a contrast of zero means it is favoured equally.

Parameterizing only the contrast means these three numbers are the parameters $\bar\theta_{1,2}$, and the reference entry is not a parameter at all. This removes the spare degree of freedom from the first question: doubling the table to 60, 10, 2, 20 gives $\log\tfrac{10}{60}$, $\log\tfrac{2}{60}$, $\log\tfrac{20}{60}$, which are the same three contrasts. Rescaling a table no longer changes its parameters.
:::

## The Ising model {#sec-ising}

The log-linear form of @sec-mrf-expfam is general. Its simplest concrete instance is the Ising model: binary variables with one parameter per edge. On a grid it is the standard MRF for the kind of problem @sec-motivate opened with, where each variable interacts symmetrically with its neighbours.

::: {.definition-block}
**Definition.** The **Ising model** is an MRF over spin variables $x_s \in \{-1,+1\}$, originally used to model magnets, with pairwise clique potentials
$$\psi_{st}(x_s,x_t) = e^{J_{st}\,x_s x_t},$$
where $J_{st}$ is the **coupling strength** between neighboring nodes $s$ and $t$ ($J_{st}=0$ if $s,t$ are not connected).
:::

Since $x_s x_t = +1$ when the two spins agree and $-1$ when they disagree, $\psi_{st}(-1,-1)=\psi_{st}(1,1)=e^{J_{st}}$ while $\psi_{st}(-1,1)=\psi_{st}(1,-1)=e^{-J_{st}}$: a positive coupling $J_{st}>0$ makes the potential larger when the two spins agree, so the model favors, but does not force, matching neighbors. Adding a per-node potential $\psi_s(x_s) = e^{b_s x_s}$ (an external field biasing each spin individually) gives the overall distribution
$$p(\boldsymbol{x}) \propto \prod_{s\sim t} \psi_{st}(x_s,x_t) \prod_s \psi_s(x_s) = \exp\Big\{\sum_{s\sim t} J_{st}x_sx_t + \sum_s b_s x_s\Big\},$$
where $s\sim t$ ranges over edges. This is exactly the log-linear exponential family of @sec-mrf-expfam, with sufficient statistics $x_sx_t$ per edge and $x_s$ per node. By Hammersley-Clifford, setting $J_{st}=0$ for a non-edge pair is precisely what makes $X_s \perp X_t \mid X_{\text{rest}}$.

::: {.callout-note}
**Practice question.** In an Ising model with three spins $X_1,X_2,X_3$ arranged in the chain $X_1-X_2-X_3$ (so $J_{13}=0$), is $X_1 \perp X_3$ marginally (with $X_2$ unobserved), or only $X_1 \perp X_3 \mid X_2$?

**Solution.** $J_{13}=0$ says only that $X_1$ and $X_3$ are not directly coupled, which by Hammersley-Clifford gives the conditional statement $X_1 \perp X_3 \mid X_2$ (they are the two endpoints of a chain, and $X_2$ is the sole separator between them, exactly the causal-chain structure of Week 2's @sec-cistructures). It says nothing about the marginal relationship: both spins are still coupled to the same neighbor $X_2$, so marginally (summing $X_2$ out) $X_1$ and $X_3$ are typically dependent, the common-cause pattern from the same Week 2 section. This is the Ising-model instance of the general chain fact proved in @sec-hc.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" .clarification title="Question: How does the general factorization give the Ising formula p(x) proportional to exp of the sum of J x_s x_t plus b_s x_s?"}
**Start from the general rule.** Any MRF factorizes as one potential per clique, divided by the normalizer (@sec-mrf):
$$p(\boldsymbol{x}) = \frac{1}{Z}\prod_{C} \psi_C(x_C).$$
The symbol $\propto$ ("proportional to") means "equal up to a constant that does not depend on $\boldsymbol{x}$", so we may drop $\tfrac{1}{Z}$ and write $p(\boldsymbol{x}) \propto \prod_C \psi_C(x_C)$.

**Step 1: list the cliques.** The Ising model uses two kinds of factor: one $\psi_{st}$ for every edge $s\sim t$, and one $\psi_s$ for every node $s$. Splitting the product by kind gives
$$p(\boldsymbol{x}) \propto \prod_{s\sim t} \psi_{st}(x_s,x_t)\,\prod_s \psi_s(x_s).$$
A single node is a clique but not a maximal one. That is allowed: $\psi_s$ can be multiplied into any edge potential that contains $s$, so the product still factorizes over the maximal cliques. Writing it separately just keeps the "pair" part and the "single spin" part apart.

**Step 2: substitute the chosen potentials.** The model defines $\psi_{st}=e^{J_{st}x_sx_t}$ and $\psi_s=e^{b_sx_s}$:
$$p(\boldsymbol{x}) \propto \prod_{s\sim t} e^{J_{st}x_sx_t}\,\prod_s e^{b_sx_s}.$$

**Step 3: turn the product of exponentials into one exponential.** Since $e^a e^b = e^{a+b}$, multiplying exponentials adds their exponents. Every factor here is an exponential, so the whole product becomes one exponential of a sum:
$$p(\boldsymbol{x}) \propto \exp\Big\{\sum_{s\sim t} J_{st}x_sx_t + \sum_s b_sx_s\Big\}.$$
This is why the potentials were written as exponentials in the first place: a product of many factors becomes a sum in the exponent, and the sum is linear in the parameters $J_{st}$ and $b_s$. That linearity is the log-linear form of @sec-mrf-expfam.

**A concrete example.** Take the three-spin chain $X_1 - X_2 - X_3$ with invented parameters $J_{12}=1$, $J_{23}=0.5$, $b_1=0.2$, $b_2=0$, $b_3=-0.3$. The definitions turn these numbers into potential tables (values rounded to two decimals):

| Factor | Formula | Value when the input is $+1$ or the spins agree | Value when the input is $-1$ or the spins disagree |
|:---|:---|---:|---:|
| $\psi_{12}(x_1,x_2)$ | $e^{1\cdot x_1x_2}$ | $e^{1}=2.72$ | $e^{-1}=0.37$ |
| $\psi_{23}(x_2,x_3)$ | $e^{0.5\,x_2x_3}$ | $e^{0.5}=1.65$ | $e^{-0.5}=0.61$ |
| $\psi_1(x_1)$ | $e^{0.2\,x_1}$ | $e^{0.2}=1.22$ | $e^{-0.2}=0.82$ |
| $\psi_2(x_2)$ | $e^{0}$ | $1$ | $1$ |
| $\psi_3(x_3)$ | $e^{-0.3\,x_3}$ | $e^{-0.3}=0.74$ | $e^{0.3}=1.35$ |

Both edges favour agreement, the first more strongly. $X_1$ leans towards $+1$, $X_3$ leans towards $-1$, and $X_2$ has no lean of its own.

Now evaluate the setting $\boldsymbol{x}=(+1,+1,-1)$ both ways. As a product of the five matching table entries:
$$\psi_{12}(+1,+1)\,\psi_{23}(+1,-1)\,\psi_1(+1)\,\psi_2(+1)\,\psi_3(-1) = e^{1}\cdot e^{-0.5}\cdot e^{0.2}\cdot 1\cdot e^{0.3}.$$
As one exponential of the sum from Step 3:
$$J_{12}x_1x_2 + J_{23}x_2x_3 + b_1x_1 + b_2x_2 + b_3x_3 = 1 - 0.5 + 0.2 + 0 + 0.3 = 1.0.$$
Both give $e^{1.0}\approx 2.72$, which is Step 3 in action: the product of the factors equals $e$ raised to the sum of their exponents.

This number is not yet a probability. Repeating the calculation for all $2^3=8$ settings and adding the results gives $Z\approx 14.54$, so
$$p(+1,+1,-1) = \frac{e^{1.0}}{Z} \approx \frac{2.72}{14.54} \approx 0.19.$$
For comparison, the setting $(-1,-1,-1)$ has exponent $1+0.5-0.2+0+0.3=1.6$, the largest of the eight, so it is the most likely setting ($e^{1.6}/Z\approx 0.34$). All three spins agree, which both couplings reward, and the pull of $b_1$ towards $+1$ is too weak to outweigh that.
:::

## Gaussian graphical models {#sec-ggm}

The Ising model is the standard pairwise MRF for discrete variables. MRFs are not limited to discrete variables, though. For continuous variables, the multivariate Gaussian gives a pairwise MRF whose edges correspond directly to nonzero entries of a matrix, and it is again an exponential family.

Recall the multivariate normal: for $X=(X_1,\dots,X_m)$, mean vector $\mu\in\mathbb{R}^m$, and a symmetric positive definite covariance matrix $\Sigma$ (meaning $u^\top \Sigma u > 0$ for every nonzero $u$), we write $X\sim N_m(\mu,\Sigma)$ if
$$f(\boldsymbol{x};\mu,\Sigma) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{m/2}(\det\Sigma)^{1/2}}$$
$$\times\exp\!\left(-\tfrac{1}{2}(\boldsymbol{x}-\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\boldsymbol{x}-\mu)\right),$$
with $\mathbb{E}[X]=\mu$ and $\mathrm{var}(X)=\Sigma$. Splitting $X$ into two blocks $X=(X_A,X_B)$ with $\mu=(\mu_A,\mu_B)$ and $\Sigma = \begin{bmatrix}\Sigma_{AA} & \Sigma_{AB}\\ \Sigma_{BA} & \Sigma_{BB}\end{bmatrix}$, the marginal is again Gaussian, $X_A \sim N(\mu_A,\Sigma_{AA})$, and the conditional is
$$X_A \mid X_B=x_B \sim N\big(\mu_A + \Sigma_{AB}\Sigma_{BB}^{-1}(x_B-\mu_B),\; \Sigma_{AA}-\Sigma_{AB}\Sigma_{BB}^{-1}\Sigma_{BA}\big),$$
where the conditional covariance does not depend on the observed value $x_B$, only on which variables were observed.

**Reading independence off $\Sigma$.** Marginal independence is simple: $X_i \perp X_j$ if and only if $\Sigma_{ij}=0$. Conditioning on everything else is more useful for graphical models, and it is governed not by $\Sigma$ but by its inverse. Let $K = \Sigma^{-1}$, the **precision matrix**. Writing $R = V\setminus\{i,j\}$ for every other variable, the following are equivalent: $X_i \perp X_j \mid X_R$; $\Sigma_{ij} - \Sigma_{i,R}\Sigma_{R,R}^{-1}\Sigma_{R,j} = 0$; and $(\Sigma^{-1})_{ij} = K_{ij} = 0$. The last equivalence is the useful one: a single entry of the precision matrix tells us whether two variables are conditionally independent given everything else, with no matrix inversion needed per pair.

::: {.definition-block}
**Definition.** A **Gaussian graphical model** represents $X\sim N(\mu,\Sigma)$ with precision matrix $K=\Sigma^{-1}$ as an undirected graph on the coordinates of $X$, with an edge between $i$ and $j$ exactly when $K_{ij}\neq 0$. Writing out the density in terms of $K$,
$$p(\boldsymbol{x}\mid\mu,\Sigma) \propto \prod_s e^{-\frac{1}{2}K_{ss}(x_s-\mu_s)^2} \prod_{s<t} e^{-K_{st}(x_s-\mu_s)(x_t-\mu_t)},$$
so $K_{ij}=0$ if and only if $X_i \perp X_j \mid X_{\text{rest}}$, matching the Hammersley-Clifford statement of @sec-hc.
:::

**Figure 6.** A precision matrix's nonzero pattern (shaded cells; diagonal is always nonzero) determines the graph edges directly: here $K_{12},K_{23},K_{34},K_{45},K_{15}$ are nonzero and every other off-diagonal entry is zero, giving the 5-cycle $1\text{-}2\text{-}3\text{-}4\text{-}5\text{-}1$.

::: {.callout-note}
**Practice question.** For the precision matrix in Figure 6, is $X_1 \perp X_3$? Is $X_1 \perp X_3 \mid X_2$?

**Solution.** Marginal independence is governed by $\Sigma$, not $K$, so the zero pattern of $K$ alone does not answer the first question; in general $\Sigma_{13}\neq 0$ even though $K_{13}=0$, since matrix inversion mixes entries. For the conditional question, $K_{13}=0$ directly gives $X_1 \perp X_3 \mid X_{\text{rest}} = X_1 \perp X_3 \mid \{X_2,X_4,X_5\}$, conditioning on *every* other variable, not just $X_2$. Whether $X_1\perp X_3\mid X_2$ alone holds is a separate, graph-separation question: in the 5-cycle, removing only node 2 leaves a path $1-5-4-3$ still connecting 1 and 3, so $\{2\}$ does not separate them and $X_1\not\perp X_3\mid X_2$ in general.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
**Homework-relevant.** Fitting a Gaussian graphical model by maximum likelihood is a direct continuous-variable analogue of Week 1's Bernoulli MLE (@sec-mle in Week 1): same "write the log-likelihood, then optimize" pattern, different sufficient statistic.
:::

Suppose we observe i.i.d. data $\boldsymbol{x}_{1:n} = \{\boldsymbol{x}_1,\dots,\boldsymbol{x}_n\}$ from an $m$-variate Gaussian with (for simplicity, after centering the data) mean zero, and write $K=\Sigma^{-1}$. The log-density is
$$\log f(\boldsymbol{x}; K) = -\tfrac{m}{2}\log(2\pi) + \tfrac{1}{2}\log\det K - \tfrac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{x}^\top K \boldsymbol{x}.$$
Dropping the constant that does not involve $K$, the log-likelihood over $n$ points is
$$\ell_n(K;\boldsymbol{x}_{1:n}) = \frac{n}{2}\log\det(K) - \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^n \boldsymbol{x}_i^\top K \boldsymbol{x}_i.$$
The sum simplifies using the trace identity $u^\top K u = \mathrm{tr}(Kuu^\top)$ and linearity of trace:
$$\sum_{i=1}^n \boldsymbol{x}_i^\top K \boldsymbol{x}_i = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathrm{tr}(K\boldsymbol{x}_i\boldsymbol{x}_i^\top) = n\,\mathrm{tr}(K S_n),$$
$$S_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \boldsymbol{x}_i \boldsymbol{x}_i^\top,$$
where $S_n$ is the **sample covariance matrix**, playing the same role here that the sample mean played in Week 1's Bernoulli MLE: it is the sufficient statistic that summarizes all $n$ data points for the purpose of estimating $K$. Substituting back,
$$\ell_n(K;\boldsymbol{x}_{1:n}) = \frac{n}{2}\big(\log\det(K) - \mathrm{tr}(KS_n)\big).$$
Two facts about this objective, useful for actually solving the maximization: $\log\det(K)$ is a strictly concave function of $K$, so the objective has at most one maximizer, and exactly one when $S_n$ is invertible, and $\mathrm{tr}(KS_n)$ is linear in $K$. Their gradients are $\nabla \log\det(K) = K^{-1}$ and $\nabla\, \mathrm{tr}(KS_n) = S_n$, so setting the gradient of $\ell_n$ to zero gives $K^{-1} = S_n$, i.e. the maximum likelihood estimate of the covariance matrix is simply the sample covariance matrix, and $\hat K_{\text{MLE}} = S_n^{-1}$: the same "set the derivative to zero, read off an empirical average" pattern as every MLE derivation so far this course, just with a matrix-valued statistic in place of a scalar one.

## Exact inference as a conditional distribution {#sec-inference}

Everything up to here has been about **representation**: which distributions a graph describes, and how to parameterize them. Having built up two families of graphical models (DAGs in Week 2, MRFs in this lecture), we now turn to **computation**, with a question common to both: given the model, how do we compute an actual number?

::: {.definition-block}
**Definition.** In a graphical model over $\boldsymbol{x}$, split the variables into $x_E$ (the **observed evidence**), $x_F$ (the **unobserved variable(s) we want to infer**), and $x_R = \boldsymbol{x} - \{x_F,x_E\}$ (**remaining variables**, summed out). **Inference** is computing the conditional distribution
$$p(x_F\mid x_E) = \frac{p(x_F,x_E)}{p(x_E)} = \frac{p(x_F,x_E)}{\sum_{x_F} p(x_F,x_E)},$$
where the joint over the subject of inference and the evidence is obtained by marginalizing out the remaining variables,
$$p(x_F,x_E) = \sum_{x_R} p(x_F,x_E,x_R).$$
:::

Both the numerator and the normalizing sum over $x_F$ require summing over $x_R$ (and, for the denominator, over $x_F$ too), so the real computational question is how to perform these sums efficiently, which is exactly what variable elimination addresses.

## Variable elimination {#sec-ve}

The definition above reduces inference to sums over $x_R$. Done naively, a sum over $n$ variables with $k$ states each enumerates all $k^n$ joint settings. The factorizations of Weeks 2 and 3 are what let us do better.

The **order** in which we marginalize out variables changes the computational cost dramatically, even though the final answer is the same regardless of order (summation commutes). **Variable elimination** is a simple, general exact-inference algorithm that applies to any graphical model, DAG or MRF, whose computational complexity depends on the graph structure and the chosen elimination order; it is a form of dynamic programming that avoids enumerating every joint assignment.

**Worked example: a simple chain.** Consider $A\to B\to C\to D$, and suppose we want the marginal $p(D)$ with no evidence, so $x_F=\{D\}$, $x_E=\{\}$, $x_R=\{A,B,C\}$. Week 2's chain rule gives $p(A,B,C,D) = p(A)p(B\mid A)p(C\mid B)p(D\mid C)$.

**Figure 7.** A chain of four variables, used to compare naive marginalization against variable elimination.

Assume each variable takes $k$ possible values. Marginalizing naively,
$$p(D) = \sum_{A,B,C} p(A,B,C,D) = \sum_C \sum_B \sum_A p(A)p(B\mid A)p(C\mid B)p(D\mid C),$$
costs $O(k^4)$: every joint assignment of the four variables must be visited. Instead, choose an elimination order and push each sum as far inward as it will go, past every factor that does not mention the variable being summed:
$$p(D) = \sum_C p(D\mid C) \left(\sum_B p(C\mid B) \sum_A p(A)p(B\mid A)\right).$$
Working from the inside out, the innermost sum depends only on $B$ once $A$ is gone:
$$\sum_A p(A)p(B\mid A) = p(B).$$
Substituting back and repeating the same move for $B$:
$$\sum_B p(C\mid B)\,p(B) = p(C).$$
So the whole expression collapses to
$$p(D) = \sum_C p(D\mid C)\,p(C).$$
Every intermediate sum here touches at most two variables at once ($k^2$ terms), and there are $n$ such sums, so the total cost is $O(nk^2)$, compared to $O(k^n)$ for constructing and marginalizing the full joint table directly: an exponential-to-polynomial improvement from exactly the same reordering trick that made Week 2's chain-rule factorization efficient (@sec-factoring in Week 2).

**Elimination ordering matters, and finding the best one is hard.** The complexity of variable elimination depends on the chosen order, since different orders leave different numbers of variables inside each intermediate sum. Unfortunately, finding the elimination ordering that minimizes the worst intermediate sum is NP-hard in general, so in practice orderings are chosen by heuristics (or, in this course, simply given).

## Sum-product inference: unifying DAGMs and MRFs {#sec-sum-product}

The chain example eliminated variables from a DAG's conditional probabilities. Since the point of this lecture is MRFs, we need to check that the same algorithm works when the factors are clique potentials that need not sum to 1.

Variable elimination on a DAG is really the same algorithm as on an MRF, once we notice that a DAG's conditional probability tables are themselves just a special kind of nonnegative potential. So we give every conditional probability table (or every MRF potential) one name: a nonnegative **factor**.

Take a small DAG on four variables $X$, $A$, $B$, $C$, and suppose we want the marginal over $A$, $B$, $C$:
$$p(A,B,C) = \sum_X p(X)\,p(A\mid X)\,p(B\mid A)\,p(C\mid B,X).$$
Rename each conditional probability table as a factor:

| Factor | Conditional probability table | Variables it touches |
|:--|:--|:--|
| $\phi_1(X)$ | $p(X)$ | $X$ |
| $\phi_2(A,X)$ | $p(A\mid X)$ | $A$, $X$ |
| $\phi_3(A,B)$ | $p(B\mid A)$ | $A$, $B$ |
| $\phi_4(X,B,C)$ | $p(C\mid B,X)$ | $X$, $B$, $C$ |

The marginal becomes a sum of a product of factors:
$$p(A,B,C) = \sum_X \phi_1(X)\,\phi_2(A,X)\,\phi_3(A,B)\,\phi_4(X,B,C).$$
The table shows that $\phi_3$ does not touch $X$, so it can be pulled outside the sum over $X$:
$$p(A,B,C) = \phi_3(A,B) \sum_X \phi_1(X)\,\phi_2(A,X)\,\phi_4(X,B,C).$$
The remaining sum leaves a function of $A$, $B$, $C$ only. Call it $\tau$:
$$\tau(A,B,C) = \sum_X \phi_1(X)\,\phi_2(A,X)\,\phi_4(X,B,C), \qquad p(A,B,C) = \phi_3(A,B)\,\tau(A,B,C).$$
This $\tau$ is an **intermediate factor**. It is generally not any of the original conditional probability tables; it is simply whatever function of the remaining variables the sum happened to produce. This is the mechanical step that repeats at every stage of variable elimination.

Abstractly, both DAG and MRF inference reduce to the same **sum-product** computation:

::: {.boxed-eq}
$$p(x_F\mid x_E) \propto \tau(x_F,x_E) = \sum_{x_R} \prod_{C\in\mathcal{F}} \psi_C(x_C).$$
:::

The symbols are:

- $x_F$: the variables we want a distribution over.
- $x_E$: the observed evidence.
- $x_R$: the rest, summed out.
- $\mathcal{F}$: the set of factors, each a group of variables $C$ with its potential $\psi_C$.

The only difference between the two model types is where $\mathcal{F}$ comes from:

- **DAG:** one factor per node $i$, on the variables $\{i\}\cup\text{parents}(i)$ (its conditional probability table).
- **MRF:** one factor per maximal clique.

## Worked example: variable elimination on a Bayes net {#sec-ve-student}

On the chain of @sec-ve, every intermediate sum involved at most two variables. On a graph with more branching, an intermediate factor can involve several variables, and the elimination order decides how many. The lecture's student network shows this, using the sum-product form just stated. First, the general procedure for computing a marginal $p(x_F)$ with nothing observed.

::: {.theorem-block}
**Recipe.**

1. **List the factors.** Write the joint as a product of factors and record the factor set $\mathcal{F}$. For a DAG this is one conditional probability table per node; for an MRF it is one potential per maximal clique.
2. **Pick what to sum out.** Every variable outside the query $x_F$ gets summed out. Fix an order for eliminating them (here the order is given; finding the best one is NP-hard, @sec-ve).
3. **Eliminate one variable at a time.** For the next variable in the order:
    - collect every factor that mentions it, whether original or intermediate;
    - multiply those factors and sum the variable out;
    - the result is a new intermediate factor $\tau$ over the other variables those factors touched;
    - remove the factors you used and add $\tau$ in their place.
4. **Multiply what is left.** Once only query variables remain, the product of the remaining factors is $\tau(x_F) \propto p(x_F)$.
5. **Normalize if needed.** Divide by $\sum_{x_F}\tau(x_F)$. For a DAG built from its own conditional probability tables this sum is already 1; for an MRF it is not.
6. **Read off the cost.** Let $N_i$ be the number of variables in the product formed when eliminating variable $i$. The largest $N_i$ sets the cost.
:::

**Figure 8.** A Bayes net over Coherence $C$, Difficulty $D$, Intelligence $I$, Grade $G$, SAT $S$, Letter $L$, Job $J$, and Happiness $H$.

This graph gives the factorization
$$p(C,D,I,G,S,L,H,J) = p(C)p(D\mid C)p(I)\,p(G\mid D,I)p(L\mid G)p(S\mid I)p(J\mid S,L)p(H\mid J,G).$$
Reading off one factor per node (its own conditional probability table), $\mathcal{F} = \big\{\{C\},\{C,D\},\{I\},\{G,D,I\},\{L,G\},\{S,I\},\{J,S,L\},\{H,J,G\}\big\}$, so $m=|\mathcal{F}|=8$.

Suppose we want $p(J)$, the probability of getting a job, with the elimination order $C,D,I,H,G,S,L$ (an ordering the instructor supplies; finding an optimal one is the NP-hard problem from @sec-ve). Eliminate $C$ first: it appears only in $\psi(C)$ and $\psi(C,D)$, so
$$\sum_C \psi(C)\,\psi(C,D) = \tau(D).$$
Eliminate $D$ next, in $\psi(G,D,I)$ and the new $\tau(D)$:
$$\sum_D \psi(G,D,I)\,\tau(D) = \tau(G,I).$$
Eliminate $I$, in $\psi(S,I)$, $\psi(I)$, and $\tau(G,I)$:
$$\sum_I \psi(S,I)\,\psi(I)\,\tau(G,I) = \tau(S,G).$$
Eliminate $H$, which appears only in $\psi(H,G,J)$:
$$\sum_H \psi(H,G,J) = \tau(G,J).$$
Eliminate $G$, now present in $\psi(L,G)$, $\tau(S,G)$, and $\tau(G,J)$:
$$\sum_G \psi(L,G)\,\tau(S,G)\,\tau(G,J) = \tau(J,L,S).$$
Eliminate $S$, in $\psi(J,L,S)$ and $\tau(J,L,S)$:
$$\sum_S \psi(J,L,S)\,\tau(J,L,S) = \tau(J,L).$$
Finally eliminate $L$:
$$\sum_L \tau(J,L) = \tau(J).$$
The result, $\tau(J)$, is proportional to $p(J)$; since $Z=1$ for a DAG's own conditional probability tables (they are already properly normalized), no further rescaling is needed here, though for a general MRF the final $\tau$ would still require dividing by $\sum_{x_F}\tau(x_F)$ to become an actual probability.

**Reading off the complexity.** Each sum above is labeled by how many variables appear inside it: $\sum_C$ has $N_C=2$ (namely $C,D$), $\sum_D$ has $N_D=3$ ($G,D,I$), $\sum_I$ has $N_I=3$ ($S,I,G$), $\sum_H$ has $N_H=3$ ($H,G,J$), $\sum_G$ has $N_G=4$ ($L,G,S,J$, the largest), $\sum_S$ has $N_S=3$, and $\sum_L$ has $N_L=2$. The complexity of variable elimination under a given ordering is
$$O\big(m\,k^{N_{\max}}\big), \qquad N_{\max}=\max_i N_i,$$
where $m$ is the number of initial factors and $k$ is the (assumed common) number of states per variable. Here $N_{\max}=4$ (achieved at the $G$-elimination step), so the cost of this particular ordering is $O(8k^4)$: substantially better than enumerating the full 8-variable joint, but not as good as the chain example of @sec-ve, because this graph has a genuinely more complex dependency structure than a simple chain.

## Variable elimination with evidence {#sec-ve-evidence}

Inference as defined in @sec-inference usually conditions on observed evidence $x_E$, but the student-network example computed a marginal with nothing observed. Reintroducing evidence changes only which variable is fixed rather than summed. The general procedure for a posterior $p(x_F\mid \bar x_E)$, where $\bar x_E$ are the observed values:

::: {.theorem-block}
**Recipe.**

1. **Split the variables.** Sort them into the query $x_F$, the evidence $x_E$, and the rest $x_R$.
2. **Clamp the evidence.** Substitute the observed values $\bar x_E$ into every factor that mentions an evidence variable. Those factors now depend only on their other variables. Evidence variables are never summed over.
3. **Eliminate the rest.** Run the recipe from @sec-ve-student over $x_R$ only. The result is $\tau(x_F) = p(x_F, \bar x_E)$. A factor that sums to 1 over the variable being eliminated, such as the conditional probability table of an unobserved leaf, drops out as a 1.
4. **Normalize.** Divide by the sum over the query:
$$p(x_F\mid \bar x_E) = \frac{\tau(x_F)}{\sum_{x_F}\tau(x_F)}.$$
This step is needed even for a DAG, because the denominator equals $p(\bar x_E)$, not 1.
:::

**Worked example.** Take the DAG $X_1 \to X_2 \to X_4$, $X_1 \to X_3 \to X_5 \to X_6$, $X_2 \to X_6$ (so $X_6$ has two parents, $X_2$ and $X_5$), giving $p(x_1,\dots,x_6) = p(x_1)p(x_2\mid x_1)p(x_3\mid x_1)p(x_4\mid x_2)p(x_5\mid x_3)p(x_6\mid x_2,x_5)$. Suppose $X_6=\bar x_6$ is observed and we want $p(X_1\mid \bar x_6)$, so $x_F=\{x_1\}$, $x_E=\{x_6\}$, $x_R=\{x_2,x_3,x_4,x_5\}$. By the definition in @sec-inference,
$$p(x_1\mid \bar x_6) = \frac{p(x_1,\bar x_6)}{\sum_{x_1} p(x_1,\bar x_6)}.$$
Computing the numerator by variable elimination in the order $5,4,3,2$ (the nested sums below run from $x_2$ outermost to $x_5$ innermost) (the observed value $\bar x_6$ is simply substituted into $p(x_6\mid x_2,x_5)$ wherever it appears, rather than summed over):
$$p(x_1,\bar x_6) = p(x_1)\sum_{x_2} p(x_2\mid x_1)\sum_{x_3} p(x_3\mid x_1)\sum_{x_4} p(x_4\mid x_2)\sum_{x_5} p(x_5\mid x_3)\,p(\bar x_6\mid x_2,x_5).$$
The innermost sum over $x_5$ produces a new factor depending on $x_2,x_3$:
$$\sum_{x_5} p(x_5\mid x_3)\,p(\bar x_6\mid x_2,x_5) = p(\bar x_6\mid x_2,x_3).$$

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" .clarification title="Question: Why does summing over x5 give p(x6 | x2, x3)?"}
**Fast test procedure.** To sum out a variable $x_s$ from a product of DAG conditionals:

1. **Find the factors that contain $x_s$.** These are $x_s$'s own table and the tables of its children.
2. **If $x_s$ appears in no factor except its own table, drop that table.** A conditional summed over its own left-hand variable equals 1.
3. **Collect the new factor's variables.** These are the other variables in the kept factors: the parents of $x_s$, the children of $x_s$, and the other parents of those children.
4. **Sort by side.** Query variables go on the left, along with any children of $x_s$. Everything else goes on the right.

The four examples below use the same procedure.

**Example 1 (the question above).** Summing $x_5$ from $p(x_5\mid x_3)\,p(\bar x_6\mid x_2,x_5)$ keeps both factors, since $x_5$ is a child of $x_3$ and a parent of $x_6$. The new factor is over $x_2$, $x_3$, $x_6$. With $x_6$ as the query, the answer is $p(\bar x_6\mid x_2,x_3)$.

**Example 2: no children left.** In $p(x_6\mid x_2)\sum_{x_5} p(x_5\mid x_3)$, the only factor containing $x_5$ is its own table, so step 2 drops it and it sums to 1. The answer is $p(x_6\mid x_2)$, and $x_3$ does not appear.

**Example 3: a chain.** For $\sum_{x_5} p(x_5\mid x_3)\,p(x_7\mid x_5)$, the child $x_7$ has no other parents. The new factor is over $x_3$ and $x_7$, with $x_7$ on the left, giving $p(x_7\mid x_3)$.

**Example 4: two children.** For $\sum_{x_3} p(x_3\mid x_1)\,p(x_6\mid x_2,x_3)\,p(x_8\mid x_3)$, the variable $x_3$ has two children, $x_6$ and $x_8$, so both go on the left. The answer is a joint, $p(x_6,x_8\mid x_1,x_2)$, not a product of two conditionals, because both children depend on the summed $x_3$. Its parents $x_1$ and $x_2$ go on the right.

**MRFs.** The same neighbor rule finds the variables, but a product of potentials $\psi$ has no left or right side. The result is an unnormalized function of those variables, so write it without a bar.

The steps below prove Example 1.

The sum has a factor $p(x_5\mid x_3)$ and a factor $p(\bar x_6\mid x_2,x_5)$, and the claim is that adding over $x_5$ leaves a conditional that depends only on $x_2$ and $x_3$. The idea is to read the sum as a marginal of a joint distribution and then use the graph to simplify that joint.

**Step 1: Write the target as a sum over $x_5$.** A marginal is a sum over the variables left out of a joint. Here the variable left out is $x_5$, so
$$p(\bar x_6\mid x_2,x_3) = \sum_{x_5} p(x_5,\bar x_6\mid x_2,x_3).$$

**Step 2: Apply the chain rule to the joint.**
$$p(x_5,\bar x_6\mid x_2,x_3) = p(x_5\mid x_2,x_3)\;p(\bar x_6\mid x_2,x_3,x_5).$$

**Step 3: Drop $x_3$ from the second factor.** The parents of $x_6$ are $x_2$ and $x_5$. In a DAG, a node is independent of its other ancestors once its parents are known, so $x_3$ adds nothing:
$$p(\bar x_6\mid x_2,x_3,x_5) = p(\bar x_6\mid x_2,x_5).$$

**Step 4: Drop $x_2$ from the first factor.** The only parent of $x_5$ is $x_3$, and $x_2$ is not a descendant of $x_5$. So once $x_3$ is known, $x_2$ tells us nothing more about $x_5$:
$$p(x_5\mid x_2,x_3) = p(x_5\mid x_3).$$
This works because the only path from $x_5$ to $x_2$ runs $x_5 \leftarrow x_3 \leftarrow x_1 \rightarrow x_2$, and conditioning on the middle node $x_3$ blocks it.

**Step 5: Substitute back.** Steps 2 to 4 give
$$p(\bar x_6\mid x_2,x_3) = \sum_{x_5} p(x_5\mid x_3)\,p(\bar x_6\mid x_2,x_5),$$
which is the identity we started from. The sum is not a cancellation. It runs over every value of $x_5$, weighting each by $p(x_5\mid x_3)$, and that total is the conditional probability of $\bar x_6$.
:::
The next sum, over $x_4$, involves only $p(x_4\mid x_2)$, none of whose terms depend on $x_4$ after it is summed out (it sums to 1), so it drops out entirely:
$$\sum_{x_4} p(x_4\mid x_2) = 1.$$
This leaves
$$p(x_1,\bar x_6) = p(x_1)\sum_{x_2} p(x_2\mid x_1)\sum_{x_3} p(x_3\mid x_1)\,p(\bar x_6\mid x_2,x_3).$$
Summing $x_3$ next produces $p(\bar x_6\mid x_1,x_2)$ (using $\sum_{x_3}p(x_3\mid x_1)\,p(\bar x_6\mid x_2,x_3) = p(\bar x_6\mid x_1,x_2)$ by the product and sum rules), and then $x_2$:
$$p(x_1,\bar x_6) = p(x_1)\sum_{x_2} p(x_2\mid x_1)\,p(\bar x_6\mid x_1,x_2) = p(x_1)\,p(\bar x_6\mid x_1).$$
So the whole computation collapses to the two-factor product one would expect from a two-node chain $X_1 \to X_6$, even though the actual graph has six nodes; every other variable was marginalized away without ever touching a table larger than three variables at once. Normalizing gives the final answer:
$$p(x_1\mid \bar x_6) = \frac{p(x_1)\,p(\bar x_6\mid x_1)}{\sum_{x_1} p(x_1)\,p(\bar x_6\mid x_1)}.$$
This is Bayes' rule from Week 1 (@sec-bayes in Week 1), rederived as a special case of variable elimination: computing a posterior for a two-variable relationship, after algebraically marginalizing away every variable that connects them only indirectly.

## Restricted Boltzmann machines {#sec-rbm}

Variable elimination is exact but can be expensive, and every MRF query seems to need the partition function $Z$, itself a sum over all variables. The lecture closes with a model whose graph structure makes some queries cheap without ever computing $Z$. As a modern application tying together the Ising model, exponential families, and Hammersley-Clifford, consider a **restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM)**: a special Ising model over visible variables $X_1,\dots,X_k$ and hidden variables $H_1,\dots,H_l$, all in $\{-1,+1\}$, whose graph is **bipartite**: every $H_i$ connects to every $X_j$, but no $H_i$-$H_{i'}$ or $X_j$-$X_{j'}$ edges exist at all.

**Figure 9.** An RBM's graph: every hidden node connects to every visible node, and there are no hidden-hidden or visible-visible edges.

Writing the Ising-style distribution with per-edge potentials $\psi_{X_i,H_j}(x_i,h_j) = \exp\{\frac{1}{l}\alpha_i x_i + \frac{1}{k}\beta_j h_j + J_{ij}x_ih_j\}$ (splitting the node biases evenly across the edges touching each node so that the product of edge potentials reproduces the full node bias), the joint is
$$p(x_1,\dots,x_k,h_1,\dots,h_l) = \frac{1}{Z}\prod_{i=1}^k\prod_{j=1}^l \psi_{X_i,H_j}(x_i,h_j).$$
Computing $Z$ exactly can be expensive (it is a sum over all $2^{k+l}$ joint settings), but the bipartite structure lets us compute the two conditional distributions $p(x\mid h)$ and $p(h\mid x)$ efficiently, without ever needing $Z$. This is exactly what the Hammersley-Clifford theorem predicts: since there are no edges between different $H_i$'s, they are all mutually independent given $X$ (every $H_i$-$H_{i'}$ pair is separated by the fully-observed $X$, the same non-adjacent-pair rule from @sec-hc), so the joint conditional factors into a per-node product, and each factor can be computed on its own:
$$p(h_j\mid x) = \frac{\prod_{i=1}^k \psi_{ij}(x_i,h_j)}{\prod_{i=1}^k\psi_{ij}(x_i,-1) + \prod_{i=1}^k\psi_{ij}(x_i,1)}$$
$$= \sigma\Big(\beta_j + \sum_i J_{ij}x_i\Big),$$
where $\sigma(y) = \frac{e^y}{e^{-y}+e^y} = \frac{1}{1+e^{-2y}}$ is the **sigmoid function**. This gives a probabilistic reading of the sigmoid activation used in neural networks: it is exactly the conditional-probability formula that falls out of treating a layer of binary units as conditionally independent given the layer below, under an Ising-style pairwise potential.

## Summary {#sec-summary3}

::: {.callout-note}
**Key takeaways from Week 3:**

- Markov random fields (MRFs) model undirected interactions: $p(\boldsymbol{x}) \propto \prod_{C\in\mathcal{C}} \psi_C(x_C)$ over maximal cliques $\mathcal{C}$. The Hammersley-Clifford theorem says this factorization is equivalent to the global Markov property, $X_A\perp X_B\mid X_S$ whenever $S$ separates $A$ from $B$ in the graph.
- MRFs and DAGs are not nested: a 4-cycle's independencies cannot be captured by any DAG, and explaining-away cannot be captured by any MRF.
- MRFs are exponential families when potentials are log-linear; a minimal representation drops one redundant coordinate per clique. The Ising model and Gaussian graphical models (where $K_{ij}=0 \iff X_i\perp X_j\mid X_{\text{rest}}$ for the precision matrix $K$) are the two running examples, and Gaussian MLE reduces to $\hat K^{-1}=S_n$, the sample covariance.
- Inference is computing $p(x_F\mid x_E)$ by marginalizing out $x_R$. Variable elimination does this efficiently by choosing an order and pushing sums inward; the same sum-product algorithm handles DAGs and MRFs via a shared notion of factors, and the resulting intermediate factors ($\tau$) are what make the computation dynamic-programming-style rather than exponential.
- Restricted Boltzmann machines are a bipartite Ising model where Hammersley-Clifford guarantees the hidden units are conditionally independent given the visible ones (and vice versa), giving the sigmoid activation as a direct consequence rather than an ad hoc choice.
:::

## Quick self-check

If you can explain, in your own words, why the same variable-elimination algorithm works on both a DAG and an MRF once conditional probability tables are treated as potentials, and why a bipartite Ising model makes the hidden units of a restricted Boltzmann machine conditionally independent given the visible ones, you have understood the core of Week 3.
